Daniel’s frustration lands because he’s pointing at a real failure mode of schooling: “procedures without reasons,” where students can execute a recipe yet can’t explain why it works or when it applies. But the post smuggles in a hidden assumption—that teaching *any* specific algorithm competes with learning to *invent* algorithms—when, in practice, invention is often parasitic on a repertoire of known moves. In mathematics education this is the long-running tension between procedural fluency and conceptual understanding; the most durable critique isn’t “don’t teach algorithms,” but “don’t let algorithms be *opaque*.” George Pólya’s classic problem-solving heuristics are relevant here because they frame algorithms as objects to be varied, tested, and improved rather than memorized spells ([How to Solve It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_to_Solve_It)).

The “比字句” example is especially telling: Daniel reads the taught method as symbol shuffling, yet it may be functioning as scaffolding for semantics—an explicit mapping from comparative syntax to an order relation. Patterned procedures can be training wheels that reduce cognitive load so meaning has a chance to stabilize; the problem is when the curriculum never removes the wheels, never asks students to translate the procedure back into an interpretation (“What does ‘A 比 B …’ *assert* about A and B?”), and never shows counterexamples where the recipe breaks. Daniel would sharpen his critique by distinguishing “algorithm as invariant-preserving structure” (a generalizable idea) from “algorithm as fixed ritual” (a brittle script). The former is exactly what it means to “come up with new ones”; the latter is what his classroom anecdotes illustrate.

A stronger reframing, then, is not anti-algorithm but *meta-algorithmic*: teach fewer procedures, but teach them as things you can derive, justify, and adapt. That means adding the missing layer Daniel gestures at but doesn’t specify: why the method works, what assumptions it relies on, how to detect when it doesn’t, and how to generate variants. Otherwise “teach kids to invent algorithms” risks becoming an inspiring slogan that quietly relies on prior exposure to the very repertoire of explicit methods Daniel wants to banish.
